articles.title: Hire the Ten-Cent AI Junior: The Delegation Playbook Small Businesses Keep Missing
articles.excerpt: When a frontier AI lab ships a new model, the usual pitch is conversation: open a chat, ask anything. Anthropic's latest cheap model, Claude Haiku 5.5, shipped with a different pitch — delegation. Ant…
articles.body: When a frontier AI lab ships a new model, the usual pitch is conversation: open a chat, ask anything. Anthropic's latest cheap model, Claude Haiku 5.5, shipped with a different pitch — delegation. Anthropic president Daniela Amodei called it "a great subagent" for "straightforward tasks that come up again and again," and the model's own docs position it for high-volume work: classification, extraction, routing. At roughly $0.10 per million input tokens — with cached prompt reads around a penny per million — it's a model positioned less as a chatbot and more as a subagent : the junior hire you give routine work to while you (or a smarter model) keep the judgment calls. Most small business owners treat AI as one assistant.
articles.author: T.M. Gunderson

articles.body: Visas pay my bills — I run an agency in Bali. The other half of my week goes into Apify Actors, and one of them is a tennis feed: pick a date and a set of tours, get one flat row per match with both players, set scores, tiebreaks and a one-line summary. I expected the hard part to be blocking. It isn't — the whole professional day of tennis arrives in a single HTTP request, no browser, no key, and a run finishes in under ten seconds. The hard part turned out to be a question that sounds too simple to be a problem: is this match over? 80 rows from yesterday Here is a real run, taken this morning (13 October 2026): yesterday's results, every tour, capped at 80 rows. 8.1 seconds end to end.

articles.title: I Fixed Microsoft's BitNet C++ Kernels: How to Run 1-Bit LLMs on Pure CPU Without Compiling
articles.excerpt: Earlier this year, Microsoft Research published the BitNet b1.58 paper, demonstrating that 1-bit ternary models {-1, 0, +1} replace floating-point matrix multiplications with simple integer additions…
articles.body: Earlier this year, Microsoft Research published the BitNet b1.58 paper, demonstrating that 1-bit ternary models {-1, 0, +1} replace floating-point matrix multiplications with simple integer additions on CPU. On paper, this delivers 70–80% lower energy draw and extreme CPU inference throughput. However, compiling Microsoft's official research repository ( bitnet.cpp ) has been broken for most developers: Hardcoded CMake compiler guards threw fatal errors under MSVC on Windows. Batch stride memory overwrites caused recurring segfaults on Apple Silicon (ARM64). The repo required recursive submodules, specific Clang versions, Python virtualenvs, or 5-10 GB Docker images.
articles.author: Abhishek Khanra

articles.title: winnow-args: yet another args parser
articles.excerpt: winnow-args is a command line parser for Rust, built on winnow. There are plenty of great crates already, why adding one more given that you have clap, bpaf and usage? All of them are quite good for d…
articles.body: winnow-args is a command line parser for Rust, built on winnow . Why another one There are plenty of great crates already, why adding one more given that you have clap , bpaf and usage ? All of them are quite good for different purposes: clap is pretty much the standard, quite user-friendly, but bit slow and not as flexible as you want once you need to parse something more than the usual --long , -l options. bpaf is way more flexible, but not built for speed. usage-rs has a very interesting approach to get the best performance while having as many features as clap. Sadly the 3 do not have at the same time the flexibility and speed I need. Speed on the cli? In brush , every builtin is a small command line: set -eu , declare -x NAME=value , printf -v var '%s' x .

The industry raced to give them tools, memory, and access to everything — then moved on to the next feature. What nobody shipped was the security primitive that makes any of it safe. Three capabilities that are individually useful but collectively catastrophic when combined in a single agent. And according to a Cloud Security Alliance survey of 235 CISOs and CIOs , 92% of enterprises still lack full visibility into their AI agent identities. The trifecta is not theoretical.

articles.excerpt: Background To talk about MRDRs, we first need to take about MADRs, which are awesome: https://adr.github.io/madr/ Building and evolving a group of MADR documents alongside your project is a great way…
articles.body: Background To talk about MRDRs, we first need to take about MADRs, which are awesome: https://adr.github.io/madr/ Building and evolving a group of MADR documents alongside your project is a great way to capture key architectural decisions, including the "why" and the alternatives, so you never need to look back later and wonder what the heck is going on with the project's design. They're also a great reference for agentic context, where they can help "pin" specific decisions that code generation and other session activities are then shaped by. But a MADR only captures the architectural decision: a specific point of the design. There's another, more ephemeral artifact that comes up again and again.

articles.excerpt: SpaceX launched 27 of its Starlink broadband satellites to orbit today (Oct. 12), the first such mission for a Falcon 9 rocket since Sept. 19.
articles.body: SpaceX just broke an uncharacteristically long Starlink launch drought. The company sent 27 of its Starlink internet satellites to low Earth orbit (LEO) today (Oct. 12), launching them atop a Falcon 9 rocket from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base at 8:28 p.m. EDT (5:28 p.m. local time; 0028 GMT on Oct. 13) It was the first Starlink mission for a Falcon 9 since Sept. 19 , which was another 27-satellite liftoff from Vandenberg. For some perspective on this recent gap: Between Aug. 19 and Sept. 6, a span of 19 days, SpaceX launched seven Starlink missions with Falcon 9s. The Falcon 9's first stage rests on the deck of a ship at sea shortly after the Oct. 12 launch. (Image credit: SpaceX) SpaceX did loft a batch of Starlinks after that, but it wasn't aboard a Falcon 9.

articles.title: The moon could turn astronauts into 'walking, high voltage capacitors' that accidentally zap spacecraft
articles.excerpt: NASA is asking for ideas to stop static electricity from zapping astronauts or critical hardware during moon missions.
articles.body: NASA is asking for ideas to stop static electricity from zapping astronauts or critical hardware during moon missions. The agency opened a "Lunar Grounding Challenge" to avoid situations where an astronaut on the moon could become "a walking, high voltage capacitor." Submissions for the $150,000 competition are due Jan. 15 and you can see the requirements here . NASA is hoping to put astronaut boots at the lunar south pole in 2028 during the Artemis 4 or 5 missions, on the first landing mission since NASA's Apollo 17 in 1972. But simulations suggest that both "tribocharging" (electric-charge transfer between two objects) and plasma charging (from ambient gas in the region) could build up electric charge on spacesuits.

articles.body: NASA experiments focused on human and plant health and drug-resistant organisms will travel to the International Space Station aboard SpaceX’s 35th Commercial Resupply Services mission for the agency from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, advancing research that benefits life on Earth and future exploration. This research supports astronaut health during long-duration missions through four investigations from the agency’s Biological and Physical Sciences division, including 3D models of the human brain, a crop disease study, a faster way to assess astronaut health, and an analysis of antibiotic-resistant bacteria aboard the space station.
